Rules and models

Source: vignettes/articles/classifiers.Rmd
classifiers.Rmd

titleclassifier makes its decisions in two ways. Most of the pipeline is rule-based: dictionaries, lookup tables and if-then rules that a person wrote or checked. Roles on 990-EZ returns are decided by a model: a statistical classifier trained on examples. This article explains each, why both are used, and how to tell and control which one decided.

Rule-based classifiers

A rule-based classifier applies explicit instructions. Each decision can be traced to a line of a table or of code, and changing the outcome means editing that line. The pipeline uses four kinds:

Kind Where Example
Text rules steps 02-06 regular expressions: \bVP\b becomes VICE PRESIDENT; a date like 6/2023 is removed and flagged
Lookup tables steps 06-08 the crosswalks: the variant “EXEC DIR” maps to EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, whose taxonomy row says CEO, general management, SOC 11-1011
Learned rules step 07 the pattern rules: a title the crosswalk does not list but that starts with MANAGER maps to MANAGER. They were found by counting how titles with each head are coded, and kept only where they were right at least 80% of the time, but once learned they are applied as fixed rules
Decision rules step 09 an if-then cascade on checkboxes, pay and hours: officer box + CEO-level title = designated CEO; a board title held under 10 hours a week for under $25,000 = board seat

Rules are transparent and stable. They give the same answer every time, anyone can read why, and an error is fixed by editing a CSV or a line of code. Their limit is coverage: a rule only knows the cases its author thought of. They also depend on their inputs. The step 09 rules lean on the Part VII checkboxes, which are the filer’s own statement of who is a trustee, an officer or a key employee.

The rules live in:

  • data-raw/crosswalks/*.csv (the lookup tables and pattern rules), loaded with get_title_xwalk(), get_title_taxonomy(), get_status_codes() and get_title_patterns();
  • the word lists (date.words, likely.titles, …), loaded with data();
  • the code of each step, in particular fix_spelling() and resolve_roles().

Model-based classifiers

A model-based classifier learns how to decide from labeled examples instead of being told. titleclassifier has one: the no-checkbox role model used in step 09 for 990-EZ returns.

The problem it solves: a 990-EZ has no position checkboxes. Without them, the step 09 rules must guess position from title and pay alone, and they miss most officers and over-call staff. But full 990 returns do have the boxes, and the rules resolve them well. So the rules on full 990s can teach a model to decide without the boxes.

How it was trained (data-raw/partvii-validation/20-role-model-ship.R):

  1. Labels. About 557,000 people on full-990 filings from a stratified sample of 2019-2023 returns, each labeled with the role the step 09 rules give them with the checkboxes.
  2. Real 990-EZ examples. 20,800 people at organizations that switched between the 990-EZ and the full 990, labeled with their role in the full-990 year and described by their 990-EZ-year filing (weight 3).
  3. Features without the boxes. Each person is described only by what a 990-EZ also reports. role_model_features() builds 100 features:
    • title keywords (PRESIDENT, CHAIR, DIRECTOR, …);
    • the taxonomy’s level, board role, domain and SOC group;
    • pay and hours;
    • the person’s rank and share of pay and hours within the filing;
    • the filing’s make-up (people, paid people, other CEO and board titles);
    • status flags.
  4. Model. Gradient-boosted decision trees (xgboost, multi-class, 151 rounds of depth-8 trees) predicting one of BOARD, CEO, OFFICER, MANAGER, PROFESSIONAL or STAFF.

The fitted model ships with the package in inst/extdata/role-model/.

system.file("extdata", "role-model", package = "titleclassifier") |> list.files()
#> [1] "feature-names.txt" "role-model.ubj"
f   <- system.file("extdata", "role-model", package = "titleclassifier")
fit <- xgboost::xgb.load(file.path(f, "role-model.ubj"))
imp <- xgboost::xgb.importance(feature_names = readLines(file.path(f, "feature-names.txt")), model = fit)
head(imp[, c("Feature", "Gain")], 12)
#>         Feature       Gain
#>          <char>      <num>
#>  1:        comp 0.26047380
#>  2:      lvlCEO 0.10857544
#>  3:  lvlOFFICER 0.08649124
#>  4:   pay_share 0.05922153
#>  5:       soc29 0.05786035
#>  6:    top_paid 0.04476602
#>  7:     brdnone 0.03602223
#>  8:   matchnone 0.03571595
#>  9:       hours 0.02388987
#> 10: kw_director 0.01855033
#> 11:        paid 0.01772674
#> 12:  lvlMANAGER 0.01745136

A model is less transparent than a rule. It cannot say “because of line 41”, and fixing a specific error means retraining rather than editing. In exchange it weighs many signals together, such as pay rank, hours and the other titles in the filing, in ways no hand-written rule does. It also makes the same decision for the same inputs: the predictions are deterministic.

Rules versus model

Rules Model
Built from expert judgment and curated tables labeled examples
Inputs title, plus checkboxes, pay and hours in step 09 title, pay, hours and the filing’s make-up; never the checkboxes
Reads the checkboxes yes, first no
Explains a decision yes: the rule that fired only in aggregate (feature importance)
To fix an error edit a CSV or a rule add examples and retrain
Used for all of steps 01-08; step 09 on full 990 returns step 09 on 990-EZ returns

Why the rules decide full 990 returns

On a full 990 the checkboxes are the filer’s own answer to the question the model would be estimating. The rules read them directly. The model was trained to imitate the rules on these filings, so it cannot beat them there.

Why the model decides 990-EZ returns

Without the checkboxes, the model does better than the rules:

Test set People Rules Model
Hand-labeled 990-EZ people (2010-12) 40 82.5% 92.5%
Form switchers, held out from training, same title in both years 10,558 95.1% 96.7%
… of whom not on the board 797 63.6% 74.0%

Most of the gain is in recognizing officers and staff: without the boxes, the rules find few officers and call too many people staff. See Performance for more.

Which one decided, and how to choose

role.method records the classifier for each person: rules or model.

data(tinypartvii)
set.seed(2)
df <- dplyr::sample_n(tinypartvii, 600) |>
  standardize_df() |> remove_dates() |> standardize_conj() |> split_titles() |>
  standardize_spelling() |> gen_status_codes() |> standardize_titles() |>
  categorize_titles()
#> [OK] standardize df step complete
#> [OK] remove dates step complete
#> [OK] standardize conjunctions step complete
#> [OK] split titles step complete
#> [OK] standardize spelling step complete
#> [OK] generate status codes step complete
#> [OK] standardize titles step complete
#> [OK] categorize titles step complete

roles <- resolve_roles(df)
table(roles$formtype[roles$role.primary], roles$role.method[roles$role.primary])
#>        
#>         model rules
#>   990       0   406
#>   990EZ   194     0

The model is used when the xgboost package is installed (it is suggested, not required). To use the rules everywhere, pass use_model = FALSE:

rules <- resolve_roles(df, use_model = FALSE)
ez <- roles$formtype == "990EZ" & roles$role.primary
table(model = roles$role.final[ez], rules = rules$role.final[ez])
#>          rules
#> model     BOARD CEO MANAGER STAFF
#>   BOARD     174   0       1    10
#>   CEO         1   4       0     1
#>   OFFICER     1   0       0     2

predict_roles() returns the model’s prediction for any rows, including full 990 rows, which is useful for checking how often it agrees with the rules.
